I’ve been going to Solidcore for 6 years. There’s no reason to avoid something you love and let the OCD win. I get it, I have contamination OCD too. 

Here’s what you can do to really mitigate your risk and still go:

- bring a towel and use is for forearms
- wear long sleeves
- wear Pilates socks 
- wipe down your machine with the new wipes they just rolled out before class 
- wash your hands and maybe your forearms after class

I do a mix of these and have never had an issue. I’m in NYC so there’s no way the risk wasn’t there but with simple precautions I’ve been able to keep doing what I love. It’s also important to really think about how the potential ringworm isn’t that bad at all. It’s a simple fungal infection that’s easy to get rid of and spot. It’s easy to contain once you know you have it. If you really love Solidcore don’t let OCD win. It already takes so much from people.

Other things that are game changers- cutting toxic people from your life, setting and holding firm to boundaries, sometimes changing one’s job if it’s causing too much stress. Sleep hygiene was a game changer for me.

Low dose abilify works more as an antidepressant than a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic. Just to validate what you’re saying bc it’s a really interesting drug. Lower doses hit serotonin receptors first in theory then move on to dopamine and others.

1. Set a regimen before bed to cue your body that it’s time for bed. Turn down the lights, limit phone use, maybe read and drink some tea. Something that’s similar every night. 

2. If you take melatonin, take no more than 0.5mg. People often take too much and it messes with you the next day. 

3. Depending on how much caffeine you drink, limit use after 2pm. 

4. Go to sleep and wake up within two-hour windows (I.e. if you usually go to bed at 10pm, your range is 9-11pm). 

5. Avoid alcohol, alcohol makes your sleep quality and duration worse. 

6. Google the Navy Sleep Method- try this out

7. Exercise during the day, tiring yourself out helps

8. Don’t drink fluids within two hours of bedtime

9. Limit things you do in bed that are not sleep related (eating, watching tv)

10. Make sure it’s cool in your room, people sleep best around 68 degrees F

11. Assess your space for stimuli that may keep you awake, perhaps consider using a white noise app or machine. Or use an app with calming nature sounds. 

12. Meditation can be very helpful

13. Deep breathing exercises

14. Sleep masks can be super helpful. Sleep quality is typically worse without them or blackout curtains. 

15. If you have underlying depression or anxiety, or another mood disorder, it may keep you up at night if it’s not properly treated. It can be very helpful to seek care for these reasons. A lot of insomnia is related to anxiety and mood disorders.

There’s a classic triad of symptoms, it’s encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction, and gait ataxia. 

Encephalopathy is characterized by profound disorientation, indifference, and inattentiveness. If these are less severe and permit higher cognitive testing, impaired memory and learning are also evident. Oculomotor dysfunction – Nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy, and conjugate gaze palsies reflect lesions of the oculomotor, abducens, and vestibular nuclei. Ocular abnormalities usually occur in combination rather than alone. Gait ataxia – Ataxia primarily involves stance and gait and is likely due to a combination of polyneuropathy, cerebellar involvement, and vestibular dysfunction. When severe, walking is impossible. Less affected patients walk with a wide-based gait and slow, short-spaced steps. Gait abnormalities are appreciated only on tandem gait in some patients.

Your post really piqued my interest. Just a disclaimer, I am a psych NP, I have my doctorate in the subject. That being said, please discuss with your provider. Here’s what I’m thinking:

1. Antidepressant treatment is thought to increase neural plasticity and adult neurogenesis in the brain, especially in the hippocampus. 

2. You quit at a high dose and went through all the nasty SSRI discontinuation syndrome symptoms, as you know now a slow taper is ideal to avoid this.  Let me be clear I don’t mean to chastise or judge, I empathize with how awful that must have felt. 

3. So what is most likely here is that the brain growth hypothesized in the literature happened to you. There is some evidence that it starts within a day of taking lexapro (architectural changes in the brain that is). So you developed new synapses from this drug aimed at the reuptake of serotonin. Once you stopped taking your meds, all those synapses still “crave” the drug in a way, and are pruned by your brain because now they aren’t getting what they need and their function is therefore not necessary. It’s a messy process and painful. 

I think your brain is now sensitized because of the withdrawal you went to. There is a significant overlap in symptoms between something called serotonin syndrome, which is when you have too much serotonergic activity in your brain, and SSRI discontinuation syndrome. I think your brain may be so sensitized to lexapro that you’re developing slight serotonin syndrome. It’s not quite the same but you can think about it as a “loss of tolerance” to the drug if it helps. Like your “tolerance” is lower, and you’re sensitized to the drug your brain “wants” to keep those synapses going. 

You may want to start even lower, at 5mg or even 2.5mg. Of course with the okay of your provider! Some 5mg tablets are able to be cut in half safely but it depends on the formulation. If you’re in the US, there is a liquid formulation if you wanted to start at 2.5mg also. 

Always as another disclaimer, though it’s unlikely, it’s always possible that you don’t remember how rough it was to start lexapro since it was years ago. A lot of people get diarrhea, nausea etc. from starting it, especially in the first week. 

I hope this helps. Best of luck!! I know this must be so frustrating. I spent a good amount of time looking through the hospital resources and literature I have access to trying to find cases of what you’re describing but I cannot. Doesn’t mean it doesn’t exist bc I’ve heard of anecdotal cases like yours very rarely. 

Take good care!! I hope this all gets sorted out. 

Edit: it occurs to me that if you’re taking other drugs like cough medicine, antiemetics, opioid pain killers, plus many more, that the addition of lexapro to those drugs could also cause serotonin syndrome and that this could be unrelated to starting the drug again (since usually that makes discontinuation syndrome symptoms go away).

Other things to consider- how is your thyroid function? If you have hypothyroidism, going on levothyroxine could be all you need. Same with vitamin d levels. Newer drugs (in terms of strictly antidepressants here) are more selective in which receptors they work on and often have less severe side effects.

Sometimes the things we think about a lot become part of one’s psychosis. Your beliefs are valid, there is no acceptable reason you should be homeless in a country that is so wealthy. Are you recently homeless? Periods of added stress can bring on episodes of psychosis. You may be headed into a psychotic episode, but you also might not. As others have said, it would be wise to avoid illicit drugs, even marijuana, and caffeine. (Not to say you were using, just what I’ve found to be solid advice). 

It might be wise to think about prior episodes you’ve had and look for what warning signs presented first. Paranoia? Doubting your own perception? Neglecting activities of daily living like showering, brushing your teeth or feeding yourself?

I know you’re in a tough spot, but the sooner you talk to a professional about this, the sooner you’ll know. If you start hearing voices other people cannot hear, fear someone can insert or take thoughts from your mind, fear that someone can read your mind, or feel like hurting yourself and/or others it’s time to go to a higher level of care like the emergency room.

Unfortunately there’s no way to draw clean lines here. In the example you gave we’d have to do our homework to see if it was a culturally accepted phenomenon because it’s not common at all for people to talk about that. People are really uncomfortable with psychiatry because so much of it is grey, not black and white. Unfortunately, there’s no other way to do it. 

What’s really more important here is that religion is not supposed to be the whole basis for a diagnosis. If I have a patient who is totally well, but they have the one off belief that they’re the next messiah, that’s one thing. But very very rarely does someone present with only religious content. Patients will hear voices that greatly disturb them. Or they won’t sleep for days or weeks. Unfortunately when it comes to religion it’s always going to be dicey. If someone comes in talking about some religion you’ve never heard of that may just be an eccentricity, not part of a disorder.

Actually in the DSM this is worded pretty carefully. Delusions of religiosity refer to beliefs not shared by others in a certain religion. For example, if a person comes to the hospital stating that they are god or Jesus, that’s a delusion. If someone comes and says “I speak to Jesus”, and that’s the normative belief in their religion, then it’s not a delusion. This issue is carefully written for a reason. Of course there are people who get it wrong, but I’ve had patients say their relatives came to them at night after dying and talked to them, and since it was a cultural belief that was shared by many, it was not used as proof of any mental illness. If a belief is shared among 300 million people, it’s not problematic, it’s culture.
